title: The Spectral Theorem, Positive Operators and Singular Value Decomposition

items.title: Self-adjoint and normal endomorphisms of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space
In an orthonormal basis, self-adjoint means conjugate-transpose symmetry and normal means commuting with the conjugate transpose
items.strategy: Translate the defining adjoint identities through the matrix-of-the-adjoint theorem and read the two operator conditions entrywise.

items.title: If the characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism splits, some orthonormal basis makes its matrix upper triangular
items.strategy: Start from a triangularising basis, read off the invariant flag, and run Gram-Schmidt along that flag so the orthonormalised basis preserves every successive span.

items.title: A normal upper-triangular matrix is diagonal
items.strategy: Compare the norms of each basis vector under the matrix and its conjugate transpose, then peel off the last nonzero superdiagonal row by row.

items.title: Complex spectral theorem: a normal endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis, and conversely
items.strategy: Use the fundamental theorem of algebra to split the characteristic polynomial, apply Schur triangularisation, and then force the triangular matrix to be diagonal by normality.

items.title: A real normal endomorphism is orthogonally block-diagonalisable with 1x1 real blocks and 2x2 rotation-scaling blocks
items.strategy: Represent the operator by a real matrix in an orthonormal basis, apply the complex spectral theorem to that matrix over C, and pair nonreal conjugate eigenvectors by taking real and imaginary parts.

items.title: Real spectral theorem: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis
items.strategy: Use the real normal classification and observe that self-adjointness forces every 2x2 block to collapse to a real scalar block.

items.title: A normal endomorphism is a sum of its eigenvalues times pairwise orthogonal projections, and each spectral projection is a polynomial in the endomorphism
items.strategy: Group an orthonormal eigenbasis by eigenvalue, write the associated orthogonal projections, and recover each projection from Lagrange interpolation on the distinct eigenvalues.

items.title: The spectral functional calculus f(T) for a normal endomorphism
For normal endomorphisms, the spectral functional calculus respects sums, products, adjoints, and composition of scalar functions
items.strategy: Compute directly on the spectral-resolution formula, using orthogonality and idempotence of the spectral projections.

items.title: Semisimple endomorphisms as endomorphisms diagonalisable over an algebraic closure, and nilpotent endomorphisms
Over a perfect field, every endomorphism has a unique commuting semisimple-plus-nilpotent decomposition, polynomial in the endomorphism
items.strategy: Choose a splitting field inside an algebraic closure, separate the semisimple and nilpotent parts on each primary component by the split Jordan calculation, and descend the resulting operators by using perfect-field separability, uniqueness, and base automorphisms of the algebraic closure to show the polynomial expressions are fixed over the ground field.

items.title: Non-negative and positive operators
Over the reals, non-negative and positive operators correspond exactly to positive semidefinite and positive definite symmetric forms
items.strategy: Apply the bilinear-form correspondence to the form (u,v) -> <Tu,v> and translate the pointwise inequalities through the self-adjoint condition.

items.title: A non-negative operator is equivalently self-adjoint with nonnegative eigenvalues, a positive semidefinite matrix in an orthonormal basis, or an operator of the form S^*S
items.strategy: Use the spectral theorem to diagonalise, read off the quadratic form from the diagonal entries, and reverse the construction by taking square roots of the eigenvalues.

items.title: A non-negative operator has a unique non-negative square root
items.strategy: Diagonalise the operator, take the unique nonnegative square root of each diagonal entry, and compare spectra to force uniqueness inside the non-negative class.

items.title: The non-negative square root of a non-negative operator is a polynomial in the operator
items.strategy: Interpolate the scalar square-root function on the finite spectrum and compare the resulting functional-calculus value with the unique non-negative square root.

items.title: The singular values of an endomorphism as the eigenvalues of the positive square root of T^*T
Singular values are well defined because the positive square root of T^*T is unique
items.strategy: Unpack the definition and appeal only to the uniqueness clause in the square-root theorem.

items.title: Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space admits a singular value decomposition
items.strategy: Diagonalise T^*T in an orthonormal basis, scale the images of the nonzero right-singular vectors to obtain orthonormal left-singular vectors, and complete both lists to orthonormal bases.

items.title: The rank of an endomorphism is the number of its nonzero singular values
items.strategy: Read the image directly from the singular value decomposition: the nonzero singular directions are exactly the basis vectors that survive.

items.title: An endomorphism and its adjoint have the same singular values
items.strategy: Take the adjoint of the singular value decomposition and observe that the same diagonal entries reappear with the left and right singular vectors swapped.

items.title: Every endomorphism has a polar decomposition T = SU with U non-negative and S an isometry on the orthogonal complement of ker T, and S is unique exactly when T is invertible
items.strategy: Build the isometric factor on the singular-vector bases, identify the positive factor with the square root of T^*T, and compare kernels to isolate the uniqueness boundary.

items.title: The operator norm ||T|| = max_{||v||=1} ||Tv|| in finite dimension
The operator norm equals the largest singular value and is attained at a first right-singular vector
items.strategy: Insert a unit vector into the singular value decomposition, bound the weighted sum by the top singular value, and attain equality on the first right-singular vector.

items.title: The operator norm is submultiplicative and satisfies ||T^*T|| = ||T||^2
items.strategy: Use the max definition for submultiplicativity and the singular-value description for the T^*T identity.

items.title: The best rank-at-most-k approximation in operator norm is the rank-k truncation of a singular value decomposition
items.strategy: Use the singular basis to exhibit the truncation and obtain the lower bound from a dimension-count intersection with the span of the first k+1 right-singular vectors.

items.title: The Rayleigh quotient of a nonzero vector for a self-adjoint endomorphism
Courant-Fischer min-max principle for self-adjoint endomorphisms on finite-dimensional real inner product spaces
items.strategy: Diagonalise orthogonally, compare subspace dimensions against the ordered eigenbasis, and evaluate the Rayleigh quotient on the extremal coordinate subspaces.

items.title: The smallest and largest eigenvalues of a self-adjoint endomorphism are the minimum and maximum Rayleigh quotients
items.strategy: Take the first and last cases of Courant-Fischer.

items.title: The eigenvalues of the orthogonal compression of a self-adjoint endomorphism to a hyperplane interlace those of the original endomorphism
items.strategy: Apply Courant-Fischer on the hyperplane and on the ambient space, comparing the admissible subspaces by one-dimensional codimension counts.

items.title: Weyl inequalities bound the eigenvalues of a sum of self-adjoint endomorphisms
items.strategy: Choose the two subspaces supplied by Courant-Fischer, intersect them, and evaluate the sum on a nonzero vector from that intersection.

items.title: The Gershgorin disks of an endomorphism with respect to an ordered basis
Every eigenvalue lies in some Gershgorin disk
items.strategy: Write an eigenvector in the chosen basis, divide by a coordinate of maximal modulus, and estimate the corresponding row equation.

title: The Spectral Theorem and SVD: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: An explicit real symmetric 3x3 matrix is orthogonally diagonalised
items.strategy: Compute the eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, assemble the orthogonal matrix Q, and check Q^T A Q is diagonal.

items.title: An explicit Hermitian 2x2 matrix is unitarily diagonalised
items.strategy: Solve for two orthonormal eigenvectors, form the unitary matrix, and verify the diagonalisation directly.

items.title: The real quarter-turn is normal and appears as a single 2x2 block in the real normal classification
items.strategy: Check A^T A = A A^T, compute the complex eigenvalues +/- i, and exhibit the real 2x2 block from the classification theorem.

items.title: A complex symmetric matrix can be nonzero, square to zero, and fail to be normal
items.strategy: Work with the matrix [[1,i],[i,-1]], compute A^2 = 0, and compare A^*A with A A^*.

items.title: The non-negative square root of an explicit matrix is exhibited as a polynomial in the matrix
items.strategy: Diagonalise the matrix, take square roots of the diagonal entries, and then interpolate the same operator as a polynomial in the original matrix.

items.title: A worked polar decomposition of an invertible matrix
items.strategy: Compute T^*T, extract its positive square root, and then solve for the isometric factor from T = S sqrt(T^*T).

items.title: A singular matrix has a polar decomposition with visibly nonunique isometric factors
items.strategy: Choose a rank-one matrix, compute the positive factor, and display two distinct isometries that agree on the orthogonal complement of the kernel.

items.title: The singular value decomposition of an explicit 2x3 matrix
items.strategy: Diagonalise T^*T, normalize the image vectors, and write the resulting U Sigma V^* factorisation in full.

items.title: The rank-one truncation of an SVD realises the Eckart-Young minimiser
items.strategy: Truncate the previous SVD after the first singular value, compute the operator-norm error, and match it with the next singular value.

items.title: Courant-Fischer is checked on an explicit 3x3 symmetric matrix
items.strategy: Compute the ordered eigenvalues and then evaluate the min-max expression on the coordinate eigenspaces and their orthogonal complements.

items.title: The eigenvalues of a principal 2x2 submatrix interlace those of a 3x3 symmetric matrix
items.strategy: Compress to a coordinate hyperplane, compute both spectra, and compare the ordered lists entry by entry.

items.title: Gershgorin disks for an explicit 3x3 matrix contain the true spectrum
items.strategy: Compute the row sums, draw the three disks, and check the actual eigenvalues against their union.

items.title: FALSE: Every normal operator is diagonalisable over its base field
items.strategy: Refute the field-free claim with the real quarter-turn, which is normal over R but has no real eigenvalue.

items.title: FALSE: Every complex symmetric matrix is unitarily diagonalisable
items.strategy: Use the worked complex symmetric nilpotent matrix, which is symmetric but not normal and hence cannot satisfy the complex spectral theorem.

items.title: FALSE: If <Tv,v> is nonnegative for every v, then T is automatically self-adjoint
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the real quarter-turn, for which every value <Tv,v> is zero although the operator is not self-adjoint.

items.title: FALSE: A non-negative operator has a unique square root among all operators
items.strategy: Use a diagonal matrix with positive entries and compare its non-negative square root with a distinct diagonal sign choice.

items.title: FALSE: The isometry in the polar decomposition is unique even for singular operators
items.strategy: Appeal to the singular polar-decomposition example, where two distinct isometries agree on the range of the positive factor.

items.title: FALSE: The singular values of an operator are the absolute values of its eigenvalues
items.strategy: Use the nilpotent matrix [[0,2],[0,0]], whose eigenvalues are both zero while its singular values are 2 and 0.

items.title: FALSE: The operator norm is always the largest modulus of an eigenvalue
items.strategy: Use the same nilpotent matrix [[0,2],[0,0]], whose operator norm is 2 although every eigenvalue has modulus 0.
